summaries.summary: Named entity recognition is important, deep learning improved models, but Armenian lacks annotated corpora, so this work creates training and gold-standard test corpora and evaluates established approaches.
Because manual named entity corpora are costly, projection-based transfer was considered effective, but it was unsuitable for Armenian due to lack of a sufficiently large parallel corpus.
Wikipedia-based approaches include Albanian gazetteers and a German rule-based system, but the latter's reliance on external tools made it nonviable for Armenian.
Nothman et al. generated a silver-standard corpus for 9 languages, Sysoev and Andrianov used a similar Russian approach, and the authors chose this model for Armenian.
The authors propose a gold-standard Armenian benchmark corpus manually annotated with CoNLL person, location, and organization categories for evaluating future named entity recognition models.
Popular entity recognition models were applied to the data for baseline results, and GloVe word embeddings were developed to train and evaluate deep learning models.
Contributions are the silver-standard training corpus, gold-standard test corpus, GloVe word embeddings, and baseline results for 3 models, all available on GitHub.
The authors used Sysoev and Andrianov's modification of the Nothman et al. approach, which uses Wikipedia article links to generate named-entity annotated token sequences.
The main steps of the dataset extraction system are described in Figure FIGREF3.

Wikipedia articles are assigned named entity classes using only an article's Wikidata entry's first instance of label's parent subclass of labels, avoiding manual classification and inter-language links.
Outgoing links receive target article types, restrictive sentence selection is relaxed by inferring aliases, and aliases are compiled for all PER, ORG, LOC articles.
Link boundaries are adjusted by removing parenthetical labels and text after commas, sometimes splitting linked text containing commas into separate named entities.
Instead of manually classifying Wikipedia articles, the authors developed a rule-based classifier using Wikidata instance of and subclass of attributes to find named entity types.
Articles were classified by their first instance of attribute's subclass of values because instance of labels were too specific and higher-level subclass of values too general.
The algorithm generated 7455 annotated sentences with 163247 tokens based on the 20 February 2018 dump of Armenian Wikipedia.
Generated data is smaller than CoNLL 2002 and 2003 corpora, with English CoNLL 2003 containing 203621 tokens, German 206931, Spanish 273037 lines, and Dutch 218737 lines.
Annotation accuracy depends on Wikipedia link quality, with errors from unlinked first mentions, wrong link boundaries, and named entities inside links not targeting LOC, ORG, or PER articles.
A manually annotated test dataset comprises 53453 tokens and 2566 sentences from over 250 ilur.am news texts, with PER, ORG, and LOC annotations in CoNLL03 IOB format.
Annotation generally followed BBN Technologies guidelines for TREC 2002, with PER, ORG, and LOC rules, except adjectival organization forms were not marked.
Entities of other categories were ignored, including ORG, LOC, or PER entities inside extraneous entity types.
Quotation marks around named entities were not annotated unless they were part of the entity's full official name.
Depending on context, metonyms and country or city names were annotated as ORG when referring to government agencies or sports teams.
GloVe word embeddings were trained on 79 million Armenian tokens from Wikipedia, The Armenian Soviet Encyclopedia, Eastern Armenian National Corpus BIBREF12, news websites, and blogs.
The authors release 50-, 100-, 200- and 300-dimensional Armenian word vectors with vocabulary size 400000, lowercased words, 15 window size, and 20 training epochs.
Experiments compared Stanford NER, spaCy 2.0, and a recurrent model with bidirectional LSTM character-based feature extraction and CRF on the data.
Stanford NER is a CRF classifier using lexical and contextual features including current word, character n-grams up to length 6, neighboring words, word shape, and sequence features.

spaCy 2.0 uses a CNN-based transition system with Bloom embeddings and residual CNNs, reportedly performs within 1% of English state-of-the-art, and was tested with 50-, 100-, 200- and 300-dimensional GloVe embeddings.
The main recurrent model with a CRF top layer combines character-based bidirectional LSTM representations with GloVe vectors, uses another bidirectional LSTM, and had biLSTM sizes 100 and 300.
Experiments used IOB tagging with 7 class tags: O, B-PER, I-PER, B-LOC, I-LOC, B-ORG, I-ORG.
The authors randomly selected 80% of generated annotated sentences for training and 20% for development, then tested models with best development F1 score on the gold dataset.
The highest F1 score came from the recurrent model with batch size 8, Adam optimizer, initial learning rate 0.001, updated embeddings, and 50-dimensional GloVe vectors.
For spaCy 2.0, 200-dimensional embeddings performed highest, and both deep learning models exceeded Stanford NER in recall while Stanford NER showed higher precision.
The automatically generated development set was not an ideal indicator of gold-standard test performance, with errors caused by incomplete annotations and incorrectly labeled non-entities.
Tested models had high precision for tokens starting named entities but failed on organization descriptor words and some location descriptors, partly due to generated data quality.
The authors release silver-standard training and gold-standard testing datasets for Armenian, emphasize the benchmark corpus, and publish GloVe word vector models trained on Armenian texts.
Evaluation results for 3 named entity recognition systems support Wikipedia-based approaches, deep learning recall, and character-extracted embeddings alongside conventional word embeddings.
Future work includes WiNER BIBREF19 to improve training corpus quantity and quality, and enriching the benchmark test set with MISC or fine-grained types such as CITY, COUNTRY, REGION.
